title: Berkeleytime — Resources
description: Resource and capacity investigation using available telemetry sources. Investigation guide: docs/observability/runbooks.md.

options.content:
Resource pressure is evidence to investigate, not proof of a cause. **Compose has no Kubernetes, node, or PVC data.** Those panels should show Unknown / No data.

Environment applies throughout; namespace/pod apply to application/container panels; workload applies to workload comparisons; service applies to backend process/API/cache panels; node applies to node panels. Dependencies have their own service identities. No limit configured is different from missing collection. [Investigation guide](https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md).

panels.title: Collection targets (1 = reachable; 0 = failed)
panels.description: Is each configured scrape endpoint reachable? This checks scraping only, not successful receiver collection or whole-stack health. In Compose, Kubernetes targets are absent. Check Targets and Collector logs when a source is missing. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Backend and Redis — available in Compose

options.content: Heap/RSS measure the Node process, separately from container memory. Event-loop percentiles describe each export window; they are not percentiles over the entire selected time range. Service, namespace and pod filters apply here.

panels.title: Backend heap and RSS
panels.description: How much memory does the backend process use? Heap is JavaScript memory; RSS includes other resident allocations. Compare with container working set and its memory limit, then investigate allocation or GC behavior. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Event-loop delay
panels.description: Is the backend pausing? Max and p99 cover each 15-second export window, sampled at 20 ms resolution. Compare sustained increases with GraphQL latency; investigate GC and synchronous work. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: GraphQL p95 latency
panels.description: Does application latency rise alongside resource use? Histogram p95 is calculated over five-minute rates, grouped by service and pod. Check traffic mix, event loop and dependency latency. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Redis operation p95 latency
panels.description: Is the backend cache waiting on Redis? Histogram p95 covers instrumented get/set/delete operations over five minutes, not all Redis commands. Compare by operation and check Redis reachability and load. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Response cache activity
panels.description: Are cache hits or misses changing? Five-minute rates count instrumented response cache outcomes. Check traffic mix and cache invalidation; idle traffic produces zero rates when counters exist. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Response cache hit ratio — traffic required
panels.description: What fraction of cache lookups hit? Denominator is hits plus misses over five minutes. No traffic or a missing counter returns no ratio, never a fabricated 0% or 100%. Check activity before interpreting. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

options.content: Unavailable in Compose. CPU is in cores (1 = one CPU core); memory is bytes. Workload comparisons require Developer 3’s kube-state-metrics. CPU limits can intentionally be absent. Workload limit lines are sums of configured limits, **not a total ceiling when any container is unlimited**.

panels.title: Container CPU usage
panels.description: Which containers use CPU? Rate CPU seconds over five minutes, then deduplicate scrape series before graphing. Namespace and pod filters apply; workload filter applies only to workload panels. Check requests and node contention. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Workload CPU: usage, requests, configured limits
panels.description: How does workload CPU compare with reserved CPU and configured limits? Requests are reservations, not caps. Partial limit sums are not workload ceilings. Check individual container limits in Kubernetes before interpreting workload totals. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Container working set
panels.description: Which containers retain memory? Container working set differs from process RSS and heap. Compare with per-container limits, then inspect growth over time. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Workload memory: working set, requests, configured limits
panels.description: How does workload memory compare with requests and configured limits? Partial limit sums are not a total ceiling. Inspect individual container ratios and configured limits before deciding capacity. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Container memory / configured limit
panels.description: How close is a container to its memory limit? Denominator is its positive configured limit; missing/zero limits produce no percentage. 85% sustained for five minutes is an investigation proposal, not a diagnosis. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: CPU throttled periods / total periods
panels.description: How often is CPU quota exhausted? Ratio sums paired throttled-period rates over paired total-period rates across container incarnations in the five-minute window. Duplicate scrapes count once per cAdvisor id. This is not percent CPU time lost. No positive denominator or unsupported counters returns no data. Investigate >10% sustained for five minutes. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Storage, nodes and network — Kubernetes only

options.content: Node data is cluster-level and ignores namespace/service/workload filters. In kind, nodes are Linux containers; these readings do not describe all macOS capacity. PVC metrics depend on storage-driver support; hostPath often supplies no volume statistics.

panels.title: PVC capacity and free space
panels.description: Which reported volumes are filling up? Kubelet volume statistics report bytes by PVC; missing statistics mean Unknown, not empty or healthy. Check the storage driver and actual volume mounts. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: PVC free / capacity
panels.description: What fraction of reported PVC capacity remains available? Divide only by positive capacity. Less than 15% for five minutes warrants investigating retention and growth; never infer PVC values from host filesystem values. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Node filesystem free / size
panels.description: How much usable filesystem space remains on each Linux node? Excludes pseudo filesystems. This is node filesystem capacity, not PVC capacity. Investigate sustained free space below 15% and check the mount path. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Node pressure conditions (1 = active)
panels.description: Is Kubernetes reporting memory, disk or PID pressure? Conditions come from kube-state-metrics and are cluster-level. Check affected nodes and scheduling events rather than attributing pressure to a specific service. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Node network throughput by interface
panels.description: How many bytes per second cross each node interface? Excludes loopback and common virtual bridges/veth; interfaces stay separate to avoid counting overlapping network layers. Check interface topology before summing. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Observability stack working set
panels.description: How much memory do the monitoring components use? Selects observability container names independently of workload and pod filters; namespace/environment still apply. Compare with limits before increasing retention or collection volume. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: Observability stack CPU
panels.description: How much CPU do monitoring components use? Selects stack container names independently of workload and pod filters. Compare scrape/query volume before changing intervals or retention. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: MongoDB and nginx — validated receivers required

options.content: Dependency panels use their own service identities and ignore backend service/workload/pod selections. In Kubernetes they honor namespace; node selection does not apply. Inspect Collector logs for collection errors before trusting an unchanged reading.

panels.title: MongoDB resident / virtual memory
panels.description: What memory does MongoDB report? Server-reported resident/virtual memory is distinct from container working set. Check source availability and compare with container limits. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: MongoDB connections
panels.description: Are database connections increasing? Gauges show active/current/available connection categories; do not add them together. Check connection pooling and request concurrency. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: nginx current connections
panels.description: Are connections accumulating at the proxy? Active includes other states, so do not sum categories. Check downstream latency and backend readiness. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md

panels.title: nginx requests per second
panels.description: How much traffic reaches nginx? Counter rate covers five minutes and may include internal status scraping. Compare with application request rates and readiness. Source: Prometheus. Collection/export delay: approximately 15–60 seconds; five-minute rates need traffic and multiple samples. Next steps: https://github.com/asuc-octo/berkeleytime/blob/main/docs/observability/runbooks.md
